Part IV (PDF) All parts

Units 9–10: the definite integral, the fundamental theorem and substitution; then the techniques for the integrands substitution cannot reach, and the integrals that model an area, a volume, work, a mass or a probability. Try a substitution first. Unit 10’s table says what to try next.

Unit 9 · Integration I: the definite integral and substitution

The notes · The problems · Name the method

Six methods. The table of antiderivatives comes straight after Riemann sums, because FTC 2 needs an antiderivative; the rest follow the order of the notes. The properties of the definite integral (splitting the interval, reversing the limits, linearity) are single moves inside them. The last method is for the integrals the others cannot reach: a continuous function such as e−x2\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}e−x2 has an antiderivative, but not an elementary one, and its definite integral is bracketed by Riemann sums.

9.1 Riemann sums and their limit

Problem. Estimate ∫abf(x)  dx\int_a^b f(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫ab​f(x)dx by a Riemann sum with nnn strips, and say whether it is an over- or an under-estimate; for a polynomial fff of degree at most two, find the right sum for general nnn in closed form and take its limit.

Method

  1. Cut [a,b][a,b][a,b] into nnn strips of width Δx=b−an\Delta x=\dfrac{b-a}{n}Δx=nb−a​. The division points are xk=a+k Δxx_k=a+k\,\Delta xxk​=a+kΔx: right endpoints for k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,nk=1,…,n, left endpoints for k=0,…,n−1k=0,\dots,n-1k=0,…,n−1.

  2. Add the rectangles, ∑f(xk) Δx\sum f(x_k)\,\Delta x∑f(xk​)Δx, listing the heights f(xk)f(x_k)f(xk​).

  3. If fff increases on the whole of [a,b][a,b][a,b], the right sum over-estimates and the left sum under-estimates; if it decreases, it is the other way round. Either way the exact value is trapped between the two. If fff turns inside [a,b][a,b][a,b], the two sums need not trap it.

  4. For general nnn, take the right sum, Sn=∑k=1nf(a+k Δx) ΔxS_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(a+k\,\Delta x)\,\Delta xSn​=∑k=1n​f(a+kΔx)Δx. Write it as a sum in kkk, expand, and pull the powers of nnn out of the sums.

  5. Quote ∑k=1nk=12n(n+1)\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\tfrac12n(n+1)∑k=1n​k=21​n(n+1) and ∑k=1nk2=16n(n+1)(2n+1)\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^2=\tfrac16n(n+1)(2n+1)∑k=1n​k2=61​n(n+1)(2n+1), and simplify to a closed form in nnn.

  6. Let n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞, and compare the limit with the value from FTC 2 (Method 9.3).

Example Let f(x)=6−x−x2f(x)=6-x-x^2f(x)=6−x−x2 on [0,2][0,2][0,2]. (a) Estimate ∫02f(x)  dx\int_0^2 f(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫02​f(x)dx with n=4n=4n=4 strips, by the right and the left sums. Which is the over-estimate? (b) Find the right sum SnS_nSn​ with nnn strips in closed form, and its limit.

(a) Δx=2−04=0.5\Delta x=\tfrac{2-0}{4}=0.5Δx=42−0​=0.5. The heights at x=0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2x=0,\,0.5,\,1,\,1.5,\,2x=0,0.5,1,1.5,2 are 6, 5.25, 4, 2.25, 06,\ 5.25,\ 4,\ 2.25,\ 06, 5.25, 4, 2.25, 0, so right=0.5 (5.25+4+2.25+0)=5.75,\text{right}=0.5\,(5.25+4+2.25+0)=5.75,right=0.5(5.25+4+2.25+0)=5.75, left=0.5 (6+5.25+4+2.25)=8.75.\text{left}=0.5\,(6+5.25+4+2.25)=8.75 .left=0.5(6+5.25+4+2.25)=8.75. fff is decreasing on [0,2][0,2][0,2], since xxx and x2x^2x2 both increase there. So the left end is the tallest point of each strip: the left sum is the over-estimate, and   5.75<∫02f(x)  dx<8.75  \boxed{\;5.75<\int_0^2 f(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x<8.75\;}5.75<∫02​f(x)dx<8.75​

(b) Now Δx=2n\Delta x=\tfrac2nΔx=n2​ and xk=2knx_k=\tfrac{2k}{n}xk​=n2k​, so f(xk)=6−2kn−4k2n2f(x_k)=6-\tfrac{2k}{n}-\tfrac{4k^2}{n^2}f(xk​)=6−n2k​−n24k2​ and Sn=∑k=1n(6−2kn−4k2n2)2n=12−4n2∑k=1nk−8n3∑k=1nk2=12−2(n+1)n−4(n+1)(2n+1)3n2.\begin{align*} S_n&=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\Bigl(6-\frac{2k}{n}-\frac{4k^2}{n^2}\Bigr)\frac2n\\ &=12-\frac{4}{n^2}\sum_{k=1}^{n}k-\frac{8}{n^3}\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^2\\ &=12-\frac{2(n+1)}{n}-\frac{4(n+1)(2n+1)}{3n^2} . \end{align*}Sn​​=k=1∑n​(6−n2k​−n24k2​)n2​=12−n24​k=1∑n​k−n38​k=1∑n​k2=12−n2(n+1)​−3n24(n+1)(2n+1)​.​ Since 2(n+1)n=2+2n\frac{2(n+1)}{n}=2+\frac2nn2(n+1)​=2+n2​ and 4(n+1)(2n+1)3n2=8n2+12n+43n2=83+4n+43n2\frac{4(n+1)(2n+1)}{3n^2}=\frac{8n^2+12n+4}{3n^2}=\frac83+\frac4n+\frac{4}{3n^2}3n24(n+1)(2n+1)​=3n28n2+12n+4​=38​+n4​+3n24​,   Sn=223−6n−43n2  \boxed{\;S_n=\frac{22}{3}-\frac6n-\frac{4}{3n^2}\;}Sn​=322​−n6​−3n24​​ As n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞ the last two terms vanish, and ∫02f(x)  dx=lim⁡n→∞Sn=223.\int_0^2 f(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x=\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\boxed{\tfrac{22}{3}}.∫02​f(x)dx=n→∞lim​Sn​=322​​.

Check. n=4n=4n=4 gives S4=223−32−112=234=5.75S_4=\tfrac{22}3-\tfrac32-\tfrac1{12}=\tfrac{23}4=5.75S4​=322​−23​−121​=423​=5.75, the right sum of (a). FTC 2 gives [6x−12x2−13x3]02=12−2−83=223≈7.33,\Bigl[6x-\tfrac12x^2-\tfrac13x^3\Bigr]_0^2=12-2-\tfrac83=\tfrac{22}3\approx7.33,[6x−21​x2−31​x3]02​=12−2−38​=322​≈7.33, inside the bracket. And Sn<223S_n<\tfrac{22}3Sn​<322​ for every nnn, as an under-estimate must be.

Pitfalls

  • Calling the right sum an over-estimate out of habit. That holds only on an increasing function; here fff decreases and the right sum is the under-estimate.

  • Summing over k=0,…,nk=0,\dots,nk=0,…,n: that is n+1n+1n+1 rectangles, one of them outside [a,b][a,b][a,b].

  • Writing xk=knx_k=\tfrac knxk​=nk​ on an interval that is not [0,1][0,1][0,1]. On [0,2][0,2][0,2] the points are xk=2knx_k=\tfrac{2k}nxk​=n2k​, and the width is 2n\tfrac2nn2​.

9.2 Antiderivatives from the table: rewrite, then read off aaa

Problem. Find an antiderivative of a sum of powers, roots, reciprocals and the table’s entries eax\mathrm{e}^{ax}eax, sin⁡ax\sin axsinax, cos⁡ax\cos axcosax, sec⁡2ax\sec^2axsec2ax, 1a2+x2\frac1{a^2+x^2}a2+x21​ and 1a2−x2\frac1{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}a2−x2​1​, as an indefinite integral or as the FFF that FTC 2 needs.

Method

  1. Rewrite the integrand as a sum of powers and table entries. Write roots and reciprocals as powers (x=x1/2\sqrt x=x^{1/2}x​=x1/2, 1x2=x−2\frac1{x^2}=x^{-2}x21​=x−2), split a quotient by a one-term denominator term by term (a sum in the denominator does not split), and take constant multiples out.

  2. Integrate each power by the power rule, xn→xn+1n+1x^n\to\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}xn→n+1xn+1​ for n≠−1n\ne-1n=−1. The exception, 1x\frac1xx1​, gives ln⁡∣x∣\ln\left|x\right|ln∣x∣.

  3. Match every other term to a table row and read off a>0a>0a>0. In eax\mathrm{e}^{ax}eax, sin⁡ax\sin axsinax, cos⁡ax\cos axcosax and sec⁡2ax\sec^2axsec2ax, aaa is the coefficient of xxx, and the answer carries 1a\frac1aa1​ (with a minus sign for sin⁡\sinsin).

  4. In 1a2+x2\frac1{a^2+x^2}a2+x21​ and 1a2−x2\frac1{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}a2−x2​1​, the constant is a2a^2a2, so aaa is its square root. The arctan⁡\arctanarctan row carries 1a\frac1aa1​; the arcsin⁡\arcsinarcsin row has none.

  5. Add a single +C+C+C. For a definite integral, leave out the +C+C+C and go on to Method 9.3.

  6. Check by differentiating the answer term by term.

Example Find (a) ∫x3−2x+5x  dx\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3-2\sqrt x+5}{x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫xx3−2x​+5​dx and (b) ∫(3sin⁡x2+63+x2) dx\displaystyle\int\Bigl(3\sin\frac x2+\frac{6}{3+x^2}\Bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x∫(3sin2x​+3+x26​)dx.

(a) Divide term by term: the integrand is x2−2x−1/2+5xx^2-2x^{-1/2}+\frac5xx2−2x−1/2+x5​. The powers give 13x3\tfrac13x^331​x3 and −2⋅x1/21/2=−4x1/2-2\cdot\frac{x^{1/2}}{1/2}=-4x^{1/2}−2⋅1/2x1/2​=−4x1/2, and 5x\frac5xx5​ gives 5ln⁡∣x∣5\ln\left|x\right|5ln∣x∣: 13x3−4x+5ln⁡∣x∣+C\boxed{\tfrac13x^3-4\sqrt x+5\ln\left|x\right|+C}31​x3−4x​+5ln∣x∣+C​

(b) In sin⁡x2\sin\frac x2sin2x​, a=12a=\tfrac12a=21​, so 1a=2\frac1a=2a1​=2 and ∫3sin⁡x2  dx=−6cos⁡x2\int3\sin\frac x2\,\,\mathrm{d}x=-6\cos\frac x2∫3sin2x​dx=−6cos2x​. In 63+x2\frac6{3+x^2}3+x26​, a2=3a^2=3a2=3, so a=3a=\sqrt3a=3​, and the term gives 6⋅13arctan⁡x3=23arctan⁡x36\cdot\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\arctan\frac x{\sqrt3}=2\sqrt3\arctan\frac x{\sqrt3}6⋅3​1​arctan3​x​=23​arctan3​x​. Hence −6cos⁡x2+23arctan⁡x3+C\boxed{-6\cos\tfrac x2+2\sqrt3\arctan\tfrac x{\sqrt3}+C}−6cos2x​+23​arctan3​x​+C​

Check. (a) Differentiating gives x2−2x−1/2+5xx^2-2x^{-1/2}+\frac5xx2−2x−1/2+x5​, the integrand again. The ln⁡∣x∣\ln\left|x\right|ln∣x∣ matters, because the integrand is defined for x<0x<0x<0 too, and  d dxln⁡(−x)=1x\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\ln(-x)=\frac1xdxd​ln(−x)=x1​ there. (b) Differentiating gives 3sin⁡x2+23⋅1/31+x2/3=3sin⁡x2+63+x2.\begin{align*} &3\sin\frac x2+2\sqrt3\cdot\frac{1/\sqrt3}{1+x^2/3}\\ &=3\sin\frac x2+\frac6{3+x^2}. \end{align*}​3sin2x​+23​⋅1+x2/31/3​​=3sin2x​+3+x26​.​

Pitfalls

  • Reading aaa off a2a^2a2. Taking a=3a=3a=3 in 3+x23+x^23+x2 gives 2arctan⁡x32\arctan\frac x32arctan3x​, whose derivative is 69+x2\frac6{9+x^2}9+x26​, not 63+x2\frac6{3+x^2}3+x26​.

  • Multiplying by aaa instead of dividing. ∫3sin⁡x2  dx\int3\sin\frac x2\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫3sin2x​dx is not −32cos⁡x2-\tfrac32\cos\frac x2−23​cos2x​, whose derivative is 34sin⁡x2\tfrac34\sin\frac x243​sin2x​: with a=12a=\tfrac12a=21​, dividing by aaa doubles. Dropping the minus sign of the sin⁡\sinsin row is the other common slip: 6cos⁡x26\cos\frac x26cos2x​ differentiates to −3sin⁡x2-3\sin\frac x2−3sin2x​.

  • Writing 5ln⁡x5\ln x5lnx. It is undefined for x<0x<0x<0, where 5x\frac5xx5​ is perfectly well defined. And the power rule cannot do 1x\frac1xx1​ at all: it would divide by n+1=0n+1=0n+1=0.

9.3 A definite integral by FTC 2; signed against total area

Problem. Evaluate ∫abf(x)  dx\int_a^b f(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫ab​f(x)dx exactly; find the net signed area and the total area between a graph and the xxx-axis.

Method

  1. Find an antiderivative FFF of fff (Method 9.2). No +C+C+C is needed.

  2. Check that fff is continuous on the whole of [a,b][a,b][a,b] (a denominator that is 000 inside it rules this out). If it is not, FTC 2 does not apply: stop. Otherwise write [F(x)]ab\bigl[F(x)\bigr]_a^b[F(x)]ab​, then F(b)−F(a)F(b)-F(a)F(b)−F(a) with both values visible, and simplify.

  3. For the total area, find where fff changes sign in [a,b][a,b][a,b].

  4. Cut [a,b][a,b][a,b] at the crossings and apply step 2 to each piece. The net signed area is the sum of the pieces; the total area is the sum of their magnitudes. State both.

Variants. A net change: the integral of a rate over [a,b][a,b][a,b] is the change in the quantity, ∫abQ′(t)  dt=Q(b)−Q(a)\int_a^b Q'(t)\,\,\mathrm{d}t=Q(b)-Q(a)∫ab​Q′(t)dt=Q(b)−Q(a). Use step 2, or steps 3–4 applied to vvv for a total such as the distance travelled, ∫ab∣v∣  dt\int_a^b\left|v\right|\,\,\mathrm{d}t∫ab​∣v∣dt, and give the answer its unit.

Example Find the net signed area and the total area between the graph of f(x)=x−4xf(x)=\dfrac{x-4}{\sqrt x}f(x)=x​x−4​ and the xxx-axis on [1,9][1,9][1,9].

Split the quotient: f(x)=xx−4x=x1/2−4x−1/2f(x)=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt x}-\dfrac4{\sqrt x}=x^{1/2}-4x^{-1/2}f(x)=x​x​−x​4​=x1/2−4x−1/2. Term by term, F(x)=23x3/2−8x1/2F(x)=\tfrac23x^{3/2}-8x^{1/2}F(x)=32​x3/2−8x1/2, so F(1)=23−8=−223,F(4)=163−16=−323,F(9)=18−24=−6.F(1)=\tfrac23-8=-\tfrac{22}3,\quad\allowbreak F(4)=\tfrac{16}3-16=-\tfrac{32}3,\quad\allowbreak F(9)=18-24=-6 .F(1)=32​−8=−322​,F(4)=316​−16=−332​,F(9)=18−24=−6. The net signed area is [F(x)]19=−6−(−223)=43.\Bigl[F(x)\Bigr]_1^9=-6-\Bigl(-\frac{22}3\Bigr)=\boxed{\tfrac43}.[F(x)]19​=−6−(−322​)=34​​. fff changes sign only at x=4x=4x=4: it is negative on [1,4)[1,4)[1,4) and positive on (4,9](4,9](4,9]. The two pieces are ∫14f  dx=−323+223=−103,∫49f  dx=−6+323=143,\int_1^4 f\,\,\mathrm{d}x=-\tfrac{32}3+\tfrac{22}3=-\tfrac{10}3,\qquad\allowbreak \int_4^9 f\,\,\mathrm{d}x=-6+\tfrac{32}3=\tfrac{14}3 ,∫14​fdx=−332​+322​=−310​,∫49​fdx=−6+332​=314​, and the total area is ∣−103∣+143=8\bigl|-\tfrac{10}3\bigr|+\tfrac{14}3=\boxed{8}​−310​​+314​=8​.

Check. Differentiate: F′(x)=23⋅32x1/2−8⋅12x−1/2=x1/2−4x−1/2=f(x)F'(x)=\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac32x^{1/2}-8\cdot\tfrac12x^{-1/2}=x^{1/2}-4x^{-1/2}=f(x)F′(x)=32​⋅23​x1/2−8⋅21​x−1/2=x1/2−4x−1/2=f(x). The pieces add up to the net value, −103+143=43-\tfrac{10}3+\tfrac{14}3=\tfrac43−310​+314​=34​, and the first is negative, as the sign of fff on [1,4)[1,4)[1,4) says it must be.

Pitfalls

  • Giving the net value 43\tfrac4334​ as the area. The integral counts the part below the axis as negative; the area is 888.

  • Taking F(a)F(a)F(a) to be 000. It is not, unless the lower limit makes it so: here F(1)=−223F(1)=-\tfrac{22}3F(1)=−322​, and leaving it out gives −6-6−6.

  • Using FTC 2 where fff is not continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b]. For 1x\frac1xx1​ on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] the bracket [ln⁡∣x∣]−11=0\bigl[\ln\left|x\right|\bigr]_{-1}^{1}=0[ln∣x∣]−11​=0 is a number, but the theorem does not apply, so it is not the integral.

9.4 Differentiating an integral (FTC 1)

Problem. Differentiate, with respect to xxx, an integral ∫f(t)  dt\int f(t)\,\,\mathrm{d}t∫f(t)dt whose limits depend on xxx but whose integrand does not, without evaluating it.

Method

  1. Find which limit depends on xxx. If only the upper one does, go to step 3.

  2. If the lower limit varies, reverse the limits, which flips the sign: ∫g(x)bf=−∫bg(x)f\int_{g(x)}^{b}f=-\int_b^{g(x)}f∫g(x)b​f=−∫bg(x)​f. If both vary, split at a constant ccc: ∫g(x)h(x)f=∫ch(x)f−∫cg(x)f\int_{g(x)}^{h(x)}f=\int_c^{h(x)}f-\int_c^{g(x)}f∫g(x)h(x)​f=∫ch(x)​f−∫cg(x)​f.

  3. In each piece ∫cg(x)f(t)  dt\int_c^{g(x)}f(t)\,\,\mathrm{d}t∫cg(x)​f(t)dt, substitute the upper limit into the integrand: f(g(x))f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)f(g(x)).

  4. Multiply by the derivative of that limit, g′(x)g'(x)g′(x) (the chain rule). For the limit xxx itself, the factor is 111.

  5. Combine the pieces with their signs. No antiderivative is needed, so this works even when there is no elementary one.

Why it works. With F(u)=∫cuf(t)  dtF(u)=\int_c^u f(t)\,\,\mathrm{d}tF(u)=∫cu​f(t)dt, FTC 1 says F′=fF'=fF′=f. The integral up to g(x)g(x)g(x) is the composite F(g(x))F\bigl(g(x)\bigr)F(g(x)), and the chain rule gives F′(g(x)) g′(x)=f(g(x)) g′(x)F'\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\,g'(x)=f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\,g'(x)F′(g(x))g′(x)=f(g(x))g′(x).

Example Find (a)  d dx∫x1sin⁡tt  dt\displaystyle\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\int_x^1\frac{\sin t}{t}\,\,\mathrm{d}tdxd​∫x1​tsint​dt for x>0x>0x>0, and (b)  d dx∫x2x dt1+t2\displaystyle\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\int_x^{2x}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}t}{1+t^2}dxd​∫x2x​1+t2dt​.

(a) The variable is the lower limit. Reverse the limits: ∫x1sin⁡tt  dt=−∫1xsin⁡tt  dt\int_x^1\frac{\sin t}{t}\,\,\mathrm{d}t=-\int_1^x\frac{\sin t}{t}\,\,\mathrm{d}t∫x1​tsint​dt=−∫1x​tsint​dt. Substitute xxx into the integrand; the factor is 111. So  d dx∫x1sin⁡tt  dt=−sin⁡xx.\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\int_x^1\frac{\sin t}{t}\,\,\mathrm{d}t=\boxed{-\frac{\sin x}{x}}.dxd​∫x1​tsint​dt=−xsinx​​. (b) Both limits vary. Split at 000: ∫x2x=∫02x−∫0x\int_x^{2x}=\int_0^{2x}-\int_0^{x}∫x2x​=∫02x​−∫0x​. In the first piece substitute 2x2x2x and multiply by (2x)′=2(2x)'=2(2x)′=2; the second gives 11+x2\frac1{1+x^2}1+x21​. So  d dx∫x2x dt1+t2=21+4x2−11+x2.\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\int_x^{2x}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}t}{1+t^2}=\boxed{\frac{2}{1+4x^2}-\frac{1}{1+x^2}}.dxd​∫x2x​1+t2dt​=1+4x22​−1+x21​​.

Check. In (b) the integral can be evaluated first: [arctan⁡t]x2x=arctan⁡2x−arctan⁡x\bigl[\arctan t\bigr]_x^{2x}=\arctan2x-\arctan x[arctant]x2x​=arctan2x−arctanx, whose derivative is 21+4x2−11+x2\frac{2}{1+4x^2}-\frac1{1+x^2}1+4x22​−1+x21​. In (a) it cannot, since sin⁡tt\frac{\sin t}ttsint​ has no elementary antiderivative, but the sign can be checked: for 0<x<π0<x<\pi0<x<π the integrand is positive, and moving the lower limit up takes a strip of height sin⁡xx\frac{\sin x}{x}xsinx​ away, so the derivative is negative.

Pitfalls

  • Forgetting the chain-rule factor: the first piece of (b) is 21+4x2\frac{2}{1+4x^2}1+4x22​, not 11+4x2\frac{1}{1+4x^2}1+4x21​.

  • Forgetting the sign when the variable is the lower limit: (a) is −sin⁡xx-\frac{\sin x}x−xsinx​, not sin⁡xx\frac{\sin x}xxsinx​.

  • Letting the constant limit contribute:  d dx∫1xf(t)  dt\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\int_1^x f(t)\,\,\mathrm{d}tdxd​∫1x​f(t)dt is f(x)f(x)f(x), not f(x)−f(1)f(x)-f(1)f(x)−f(1).

9.5 Substitution, indefinite and definite

Problem. Integrate a function that is not in the table but contains an inside function together with its derivative; evaluate such a definite integral.

Method

  1. Choose u=g(x)u=g(x)u=g(x), the inside function whose derivative g′(x)g'(x)g′(x) is also present, up to a constant factor.

  2. Write  du=g′(x)  dx\,\mathrm{d}u=g'(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}xdu=g′(x)dx, and solve it for the piece the integrand contains (for instance x  dx=12  dux\,\,\mathrm{d}x=\tfrac12\,\,\mathrm{d}uxdx=21​du).

  3. For a definite integral, convert the limits: x=a⇒u=g(a)x=a\Rightarrow u=g(a)x=a⇒u=g(a), x=b⇒u=g(b)x=b\Rightarrow u=g(b)x=b⇒u=g(b).

  4. Rewrite the whole integral in uuu. No xxx may be left. A constant may be moved across the integral sign; a function may not.

  5. Integrate in uuu, from the table.

  6. Indefinite: put u=g(x)u=g(x)u=g(x) back and add +C+C+C. Definite: evaluate with the uuu-limits, and never return to xxx.

  7. Check an indefinite answer by differentiating it.

Variants. The f′/ff'/ff′/f pattern: when the numerator is a constant ccc times the derivative of the denominator, u=u=u= denominator gives c∫ duuc\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}u}uc∫udu​, so ∫c g′(x)g(x)  dx=cln⁡∣g(x)∣+C\int\frac{c\,g'(x)}{g(x)}\,\,\mathrm{d}x=c\ln\left|g(x)\right|+C∫g(x)cg′(x)​dx=cln∣g(x)∣+C. Drop the bars only when g>0g>0g>0 is known. A stray xxx: if u=x+ku=x+ku=x+k leaves a factor xxx behind, write x=u−kx=u-kx=u−k and expand into powers of uuu. Completing the square: a quadratic with no real roots in a denominator becomes A[(x+h)2+a2]A\bigl[(x+h)^2+a^2\bigr]A[(x+h)2+a2], with AAA its x2x^2x2 coefficient; take the 1A\frac1AA1​ out, put u=x+hu=x+hu=x+h and use the table entry ∫ dua2+u2=1aarctan⁡ua\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}u}{a^2+u^2}=\frac1a\arctan\frac ua∫a2+u2du​=a1​arctanau​. Route 1 for a definite integral: integrate, return to xxx, then apply the xxx-limits (Method 9.3). Both routes give the same number.

Pitfalls

  • Keeping the xxx-limits after changing the variable, as in ∫0π/3u−3  du\int_0^{\pi/3}u^{-3}\,\,\mathrm{d}u∫0π/3​u−3du. The limits belong to the variable of integration.

9.6 No elementary antiderivative: decide, then bracket

Problem. Decide whether FTC 2 can evaluate an integral with an elementary antiderivative. When it cannot, say why, say what antiderivative there is, and estimate the definite integral from Riemann sums.

Method

  1. Look for an inside function whose derivative is also present, up to a constant. If there is one, the integral is elementary: substitute (Method 9.5) and evaluate by FTC 2.

  2. If the integrand is one the notes name, e−x2\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}e−x2, sin⁡xx\frac{\sin x}{x}xsinx​, sin⁡(x2)\sin(x^2)sin(x2), exx\frac{\mathrm{e}^x}{x}xex​ or 1ln⁡x\frac1{\ln x}lnx1​, it has no elementary antiderivative (Liouville). Quote this. It still has an antiderivative, its area function F(x)=∫axf(t)  dtF(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,\,\mathrm{d}tF(x)=∫ax​f(t)dt (FTC 1). What it lacks is a formula, so FTC 2 has nothing to substitute into.

  3. Estimate the definite integral by the left and right sums with nnn strips (Method 9.1, steps 1–2).

  4. Decide the direction of each sum from monotonicity (Method 9.1, step 3), and state the bracket, rounding outwards. More strips tighten it.

Example Of P=∫24 dxln⁡xP=\displaystyle\int_2^4\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{\ln x}P=∫24​lnxdx​ and Q=∫24 dxxln⁡xQ=\displaystyle\int_2^4\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x\ln x}Q=∫24​xlnxdx​, one can be evaluated by FTC 2. Evaluate it. For the other, say why FTC 2 cannot, and bracket it with n=4n=4n=4 strips.

QQQ: the inside function is u=ln⁡xu=\ln xu=lnx, and its derivative 1x\frac1xx1​ is present. So  du= dxx\,\mathrm{d}u=\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x}du=xdx​, and the limits are x=2 ⇒ u=ln⁡2,x=4 ⇒ u=ln⁡4=2ln⁡2.x=2\ \Rightarrow\ u=\ln 2,\qquad\allowbreak x=4\ \Rightarrow\ u=\ln 4=2\ln 2 .x=2 ⇒ u=ln2,x=4 ⇒ u=ln4=2ln2. Hence Q=∫ln⁡22ln⁡2 duu=ln⁡(2ln⁡2)−ln⁡(ln⁡2)=ln⁡2≈0.693.\begin{align*} Q&=\int_{\ln 2}^{2\ln 2}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}u}{u}\\ &=\ln(2\ln 2)-\ln(\ln 2)\\ &=\boxed{\ln 2}\approx0.693 . \end{align*}Q​=∫ln22ln2​udu​=ln(2ln2)−ln(ln2)=ln2​≈0.693.​

PPP: 1ln⁡x\frac1{\ln x}lnx1​ is on the notes’ list, and no factor 1x\frac1xx1​ is present. (Forcing u=ln⁡xu=\ln xu=lnx gives  dx=eu  du\,\mathrm{d}x=\mathrm{e}^u\,\,\mathrm{d}udx=eudu and turns PPP into ∫euu  du\int\frac{\mathrm{e}^u}{u}\,\,\mathrm{d}u∫ueu​du, another entry on the list.) So there is no elementary antiderivative, only the area function F(x)=∫2x dtln⁡tF(x)=\int_2^x\frac{\,\mathrm{d}t}{\ln t}F(x)=∫2x​lntdt​. With Δx=0.5\Delta x=0.5Δx=0.5, the heights at x=2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4x=2,\,2.5,\,3,\,3.5,\,4x=2,2.5,3,3.5,4 are 1.4427, 1.0914, 0.9102, 0.7982, 0.72131.4427,\ 1.0914,\ 0.9102,\ 0.7982,\ 0.72131.4427, 1.0914, 0.9102, 0.7982, 0.7213. The first four add to 4.24254.24254.2425 and the last four to 3.52113.52113.5211, so left=0.5⋅4.2425≈2.1213,\text{left}=0.5\cdot4.2425\approx2.1213,left=0.5⋅4.2425≈2.1213, right=0.5⋅3.5211≈1.7606.\text{right}=0.5\cdot3.5211\approx1.7606 .right=0.5⋅3.5211≈1.7606. ln⁡x\ln xlnx increases and is positive on [2,4][2,4][2,4], so 1ln⁡x\frac1{\ln x}lnx1​ decreases: the left sum is the over-estimate. Pitfalls

  • Reading “no elementary antiderivative” as “no antiderivative”. PPP has one, F(x)=∫2x dtln⁡tF(x)=\int_2^x\frac{\,\mathrm{d}t}{\ln t}F(x)=∫2x​lntdt​ with F′(x)=1ln⁡xF'(x)=\frac1{\ln x}F′(x)=lnx1​. What it lacks is a formula.

  • Dividing by the derivative of the inside. ∫e−x2  dx\int\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫e−x2dx is not e−x2−2x\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}}{-2x}−2xe−x2​: its derivative is e−x2(1+12x2)\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}\bigl(1+\frac1{2x^2}\bigr)e−x2(1+2x21​). Substitution needs the derivative present as a factor; you cannot divide by it.

  • Saying “no” because a substitution fails. Only the functions the notes list may be quoted as non-elementary. x exx\,\mathrm{e}^{x}xex offers no substitution, yet it integrates, by integration by parts, in Unit 10.

Unit 10 · Integration II: techniques and applications

The notes · The problems · Name the method

Seven methods: four techniques of integration, then three uses of the integral. On this unit choosing the technique is most of the work. Look for a substitution first (Method 9.5); when there is none, the shape of the integrand says what to try next.

10.1 Integration by parts

Problem. Integrate a product of two different kinds of function, such as a polynomial times an exponential, or a lone logarithm or inverse trigonometric function, such as ln⁡x\ln xlnx.

Method

  1. Name the choice by LIATE: uuu is the factor that comes first in Logarithm, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential, and the rest is v′v'v′. For a lone function such as ln⁡x\ln xlnx or arctan⁡x\arctan xarctanx, take v′=1v'=1v′=1.

  2. Write down u′u'u′ and vvv.

  3. Apply ∫uv′  dx=uv−∫u′v  dx\int uv'\,\,\mathrm{d}x=uv-\int u'v\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫uv′dx=uv−∫u′vdx. For a definite integral the first term is [uv]ab\bigl[uv\bigr]_a^b[uv]ab​.

  4. Evaluate the new integral. If it needs parts again, repeat with the same kind of choice.

  5. If the integral you started with comes back, call it III and solve for III algebraically. Do not keep going.

  6. Add +C+C+C to an indefinite result.

Example Evaluate (a) ∫0π/4xsec⁡2x  dx\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}x\sec^2x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫0π/4​xsec2xdx and (b) ∫sin⁡(ln⁡x)  dx\displaystyle\int\sin(\ln x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫sin(lnx)dx for x>0x>0x>0.

(a) LIATE: xxx (algebraic) before sec⁡2x\sec^2xsec2x (trigonometric), so u=xu=xu=x, v′=sec⁡2xv'=\sec^2xv′=sec2x, giving u′=1u'=1u′=1 and v=tan⁡xv=\tan xv=tanx. Call the integral JJJ. Then J=[xtan⁡x]0π/4−∫0π/4tan⁡x  dx=π4−[ln⁡∣sec⁡x∣]0π/4=π4−ln⁡2,\begin{align*} J&=\bigl[x\tan x\bigr]_0^{\pi/4}-\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan x\,\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &=\tfrac\pi4-\bigl[\ln\left|\sec x\right|\bigr]_0^{\pi/4} =\tfrac\pi4-\ln\sqrt2 , \end{align*}J​=[xtanx]0π/4​−∫0π/4​tanxdx=4π​−[ln∣secx∣]0π/4​=4π​−ln2​,​ that is, π4−12ln⁡2≈0.439\boxed{\tfrac\pi4-\tfrac12\ln2}\approx0.4394π​−21​ln2​≈0.439.

(b) A lone function, so try v′=1v'=1v′=1, as for ln⁡x\ln xlnx: take u=sin⁡(ln⁡x)u=\sin(\ln x)u=sin(lnx), v′=1v'=1v′=1: then u′=cos⁡(ln⁡x)/xu'=\cos(\ln x)/xu′=cos(lnx)/x and v=xv=xv=x, and the xxx cancels: I=∫sin⁡(ln⁡x)  dx=xsin⁡(ln⁡x)−∫cos⁡(ln⁡x)  dx.I=\int\sin(\ln x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x=x\sin(\ln x)-\int\cos(\ln x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x .I=∫sin(lnx)dx=xsin(lnx)−∫cos(lnx)dx. Parts again, the same way (u=cos⁡(ln⁡x)u=\cos(\ln x)u=cos(lnx), v′=1v'=1v′=1, u′=−sin⁡(ln⁡x)/xu'=-\sin(\ln x)/xu′=−sin(lnx)/x): ∫cos⁡(ln⁡x)  dx=xcos⁡(ln⁡x)+I.\int\cos(\ln x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x=x\cos(\ln x)+I .∫cos(lnx)dx=xcos(lnx)+I. The original integral has come back. Substitute and solve for III: I=xsin⁡(ln⁡x)−xcos⁡(ln⁡x)−I,I=x\sin(\ln x)-x\cos(\ln x)-I ,I=xsin(lnx)−xcos(lnx)−I, so 2I=x(sin⁡(ln⁡x)−cos⁡(ln⁡x))2I=x\bigl(\sin(\ln x)-\cos(\ln x)\bigr)2I=x(sin(lnx)−cos(lnx)) and I=x2(sin⁡(ln⁡x)−cos⁡(ln⁡x))+CI=\boxed{\tfrac x2\bigl(\sin(\ln x)-\cos(\ln x)\bigr)+C}I=2x​(sin(lnx)−cos(lnx))+C​

Check. Differentiate. In (a),  d dx(xtan⁡x−ln⁡∣sec⁡x∣)=tan⁡x+xsec⁡2x−tan⁡x=xsec⁡2x\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\bigl(x\tan x-\ln\left|\sec x\right|\bigr) =\tan x+x\sec^2x-\tan x=x\sec^2xdxd​(xtanx−ln∣secx∣)=tanx+xsec2x−tanx=xsec2x. In (b), the product rule gives 12(sin⁡(ln⁡x)−cos⁡(ln⁡x))+12(cos⁡(ln⁡x)+sin⁡(ln⁡x))=sin⁡(ln⁡x)\tfrac12\bigl(\sin(\ln x)-\cos(\ln x)\bigr)+\tfrac12\bigl(\cos(\ln x)+\sin(\ln x)\bigr) =\sin(\ln x)21​(sin(lnx)−cos(lnx))+21​(cos(lnx)+sin(lnx))=sin(lnx).

Pitfalls

  • Choosing the other way round. In (a), u=sec⁡2xu=\sec^2xu=sec2x and v′=xv'=xv′=x give ∫12x2⋅2sec⁡2xtan⁡x  dx\int\tfrac12x^2\cdot2\sec^2x\tan x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫21​x2⋅2sec2xtanxdx, worse than the integral you started with.

  • Applying parts a third time in (b). Once III reappears, the next round only undoes the last one; solve for III instead.

10.2 Partial fractions, branched by the denominator

Problem. Integrate a rational function P(x)Q(x)\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}Q(x)P(x)​, a polynomial over a polynomial. A power of an irreducible quadratic, such as 1/(x2+1)21/(x^2+1)^21/(x2+1)2, is not split here: use Method 10.4.

Method

  1. Is it proper? If the degree of PPP is at least that of QQQ, divide first: a polynomial plus a proper remainder.

  2. Factor QQQ into linear factors and irreducible quadratics (negative discriminant). If QQQ is a single irreducible quadratic and PPP is a constant, there is nothing to split: complete the square, (x+p)2+q(x+p)^2+q(x+p)2+q, and put u=x+pu=x+pu=x+p.

  3. Write the template: Aax+b\dfrac{A}{ax+b}ax+bA​ for each linear factor; one term for each power of a repeated linear factor, up to the highest; and Ax+Bax2+bx+c\dfrac{Ax+B}{ax^2+bx+c}ax2+bx+cAx+B​ for an irreducible quadratic.

  4. Clear the denominators. Cover-up: put xxx equal to the root of each linear factor, which wipes out every term but one. Match a coefficient (or substitute another xxx) for each constant cover-up cannot reach.

  5. Integrate term by term: Aax+b\dfrac{A}{ax+b}ax+bA​ gives Aaln⁡∣ax+b∣\tfrac Aa\ln\left|ax+b\right|aA​ln∣ax+b∣, and 1(ax+b)2\dfrac{1}{(ax+b)^2}(ax+b)21​ gives −1a(ax+b)-\dfrac{1}{a(ax+b)}−a(ax+b)1​. Over an irreducible quadratic, split the numerator into the f′/ff'/ff′/f part (a ln⁡\lnln) and the rest (an arctan⁡\arctanarctan, after completing the square).

Example Evaluate (a) ∫x2+2x2+x−2  dx\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+2}{x^2+x-2}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫x2+x−2x2+2​dx and (b) ∫2x2+x+2(x−1)(x2+4)  dx\displaystyle\int\frac{2x^2+x+2}{(x-1)(x^2+4)}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫(x−1)(x2+4)2x2+x+2​dx.

(a) Both degrees are 222, so divide first: x2+2x2+x−2=1+4−xx2+x−2.\frac{x^2+2}{x^2+x-2}=1+\frac{4-x}{x^2+x-2} .x2+x−2x2+2​=1+x2+x−24−x​. The denominator factors as (x−1)(x+2)(x-1)(x+2)(x−1)(x+2), two distinct linear factors, so 4−x(x−1)(x+2)=Ax−1+Bx+2,\frac{4-x}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+2},(x−1)(x+2)4−x​=x−1A​+x+2B​, and 4−x=A(x+2)+B(x−1)4-x=A(x+2)+B(x-1)4−x=A(x+2)+B(x−1). Cover-up: x=1x=1x=1 gives 3=3A3=3A3=3A, so A=1A=1A=1; x=−2x=-2x=−2 gives 6=−3B6=-3B6=−3B, so B=−2B=-2B=−2. Integrating term by term, x+ln⁡∣x−1∣−2ln⁡∣x+2∣+C\boxed{x+\ln\left|x-1\right|-2\ln\left|x+2\right|+C}x+ln∣x−1∣−2ln∣x+2∣+C​

(b) Proper, with a linear factor and the quadratic x2+4x^2+4x2+4, which is irreducible (discriminant −16-16−16). The template is 2x2+x+2(x−1)(x2+4)=Ax−1+Bx+Cx2+4,\frac{2x^2+x+2}{(x-1)(x^2+4)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4},(x−1)(x2+4)2x2+x+2​=x−1A​+x2+4Bx+C​, so 2x2+x+2=A(x2+4)+(Bx+C)(x−1)2x^2+x+2=A(x^2+4)+(Bx+C)(x-1)2x2+x+2=A(x2+4)+(Bx+C)(x−1). Cover-up at x=1x=1x=1: 5=5A5=5A5=5A, so A=1A=1A=1. Cover-up cannot reach BBB and CCC. Match coefficients instead: the x2x^2x2 terms give 2=A+B2=A+B2=A+B, so B=1B=1B=1; the constants give 2=4A−C2=4A-C2=4A−C, so C=2C=2C=2. Split the quadratic term into its f′/ff'/ff′/f part and the rest: x+2x2+4=12⋅2xx2+4+2x2+4.\frac{x+2}{x^2+4}=\frac12\cdot\frac{2x}{x^2+4}+\frac{2}{x^2+4} .x2+4x+2​=21​⋅x2+42x​+x2+42​. With ∫ dxa2+x2=1aarctan⁡xa\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{a^2+x^2}=\frac1a\arctan\frac xa∫a2+x2dx​=a1​arctanax​ and a=2a=2a=2, ln⁡∣x−1∣+12ln⁡(x2+4)+arctan⁡x2+C\boxed{\ln\left|x-1\right|+\tfrac12\ln(x^2+4)+\arctan\tfrac x2+C}ln∣x−1∣+21​ln(x2+4)+arctan2x​+C​

Check. Recombine at a convenient xxx. At x=0x=0x=0, the integrand of (a) is 2−2=−1\tfrac{2}{-2}=-1−22​=−1 and the split form gives 1+1−1−22=−11+\tfrac1{-1}-\tfrac22=-11+−11​−22​=−1; the integrand of (b) is 2(−1)⋅4=−12\tfrac{2}{(-1)\cdot4}=-\tfrac12(−1)⋅42​=−21​ and the split form gives 1−1+24=−12\tfrac1{-1}+\tfrac24=-\tfrac12−11​+42​=−21​. But x=0x=0x=0 wipes out the BxBxBx term, so test (b) at x=2x=2x=2 too: 121⋅8=32\tfrac{12}{1\cdot8}=\tfrac321⋅812​=23​ and 11+48=32\tfrac11+\tfrac48=\tfrac3211​+84​=23​.

Pitfalls

  • Splitting before dividing. In (a), the template Ax−1+Bx+2\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+2}x−1A​+x+2B​ can never produce the 111 that division gives, and the equations for AAA and BBB are inconsistent.

  • Putting a constant over an irreducible quadratic. In (b), the numerator over x2+4x^2+4x2+4 must be Bx+CBx+CBx+C, with two constants.

  • Reaching for partial fractions when the numerator is the derivative of the denominator: ∫2x+1x2+x−2  dx\int\frac{2x+1}{x^2+x-2}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫x2+x−22x+1​dx is ln⁡∣x2+x−2∣+C\ln\left|x^2+x-2\right|+Cln​x2+x−2​+C at once, by substitution.

10.3 Trigonometric integrals: odd or even powers, tan and sec

Problem. Integrate a product of powers of sin⁡x\sin xsinx and cos⁡x\cos xcosx, or of tan⁡x\tan xtanx and sec⁡x\sec xsecx.

Method

  1. Classify. Powers of sin⁡\sinsin and cos⁡\coscos: if one power is odd, split off one factor of it; if both are even, use the half-angle identities. Powers tan⁡mxsec⁡nx\tan^mx\sec^nxtanmxsecnx: if n≥2n\ge2n≥2 is even, peel off sec⁡2x\sec^2xsec2x; otherwise, if mmm is odd or there is no sec⁡x\sec xsecx, peel off tan⁡2x=sec⁡2x−1\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1tan2x=sec2x−1.

  2. Rewrite the rest with an identity: sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1sin2x+cos2x=1 for an odd power; cos⁡2x=12(1+cos⁡2x)\cos^2x=\tfrac12(1+\cos2x)cos2x=21​(1+cos2x) and sin⁡2x=12(1−cos⁡2x)\sin^2x=\tfrac12(1-\cos2x)sin2x=21​(1−cos2x) for even powers; 1+tan⁡2x=sec⁡2x1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x1+tan2x=sec2x for tangents and secants.

  3. Substitute: u=cos⁡xu=\cos xu=cosx if you split off sin⁡x\sin xsinx ( du=−sin⁡x  dx\,\mathrm{d}u=-\sin x\,\,\mathrm{d}xdu=−sinxdx), u=sin⁡xu=\sin xu=sinx if you split off cos⁡x\cos xcosx, u=tan⁡xu=\tan xu=tanx for each piece tan⁡kxsec⁡2x\tan^kx\sec^2xtankxsec2x, u=sec⁡xu=\sec xu=secx for a piece sec⁡kx sec⁡xtan⁡x\sec^kx\,\sec x\tan xseckxsecxtanx. For a definite integral, map the limits, and keep the sign.

  4. A leftover ∫tan⁡x  dx\int\tan x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫tanxdx is ln⁡∣sec⁡x∣+C\ln\left|\sec x\right|+Cln∣secx∣+C.

  5. Write the result in terms of xxx, and add +C+C+C to an indefinite one.

Example Evaluate (a) ∫0π/2sin⁡5xcos⁡3x  dx\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^5x\cos^3x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫0π/2​sin5xcos3xdx and (b) ∫tan⁡3xsec⁡4x  dx\displaystyle\int\tan^3x\sec^4x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫tan3xsec4xdx.

(a) Both powers are odd, so either can be split. Split off one cos⁡x\cos xcosx and write the rest in sines: sin⁡5xcos⁡3x=sin⁡5x (1−sin⁡2x)cos⁡x\sin^5x\cos^3x=\sin^5x\,(1-\sin^2x)\cos xsin5xcos3x=sin5x(1−sin2x)cosx. Put u=sin⁡xu=\sin xu=sinx,  du=cos⁡x  dx\,\mathrm{d}u=\cos x\,\,\mathrm{d}xdu=cosxdx, with x=0↦u=0x=0\mapsto u=0x=0↦u=0 and x=π2↦u=1x=\tfrac\pi2\mapsto u=1x=2π​↦u=1: ∫0π/2sin⁡5xcos⁡3x  dx=∫01u5(1−u2)  du=16−18=124.\begin{align*} \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^5x\cos^3x\,\,\mathrm{d}x&=\int_0^1u^5(1-u^2)\,\,\mathrm{d}u\\ &=\tfrac16-\tfrac18=\boxed{\tfrac1{24}} . \end{align*}∫0π/2​sin5xcos3xdx​=∫01​u5(1−u2)du=61​−81​=241​​.​

(b) The power of sec⁡\secsec is even, so peel off sec⁡2x\sec^2xsec2x (mmm is odd too, but nnn comes first) and convert the rest, tan⁡3xsec⁡4x=tan⁡3x (1+tan⁡2x)sec⁡2x\tan^3x\sec^4x=\tan^3x\,(1+\tan^2x)\sec^2xtan3xsec4x=tan3x(1+tan2x)sec2x. With u=tan⁡xu=\tan xu=tanx,  du=sec⁡2x  dx\,\mathrm{d}u=\sec^2x\,\,\mathrm{d}xdu=sec2xdx, ∫tan⁡3xsec⁡4x  dx=∫u3(1+u2)  du=14u4+16u6+C,\int\tan^3x\sec^4x\,\,\mathrm{d}x=\int u^3(1+u^2)\,\,\mathrm{d}u =\tfrac14u^4+\tfrac16u^6+C ,∫tan3xsec4xdx=∫u3(1+u2)du=41​u4+61​u6+C, that is, 14tan⁡4x+16tan⁡6x+C\boxed{\tfrac14\tan^4x+\tfrac16\tan^6x+C}41​tan4x+61​tan6x+C​.

Check. In (a), split off sin⁡x\sin xsinx instead: u=cos⁡xu=\cos xu=cosx maps 0↦10\mapsto10↦1 and π2↦0\tfrac\pi2\mapsto02π​↦0, and the minus sign from  du\,\mathrm{d}udu turns the limits round, giving ∫01(1−u2)2u3  du=14−13+18=124\int_0^1(1-u^2)^2u^3\,\,\mathrm{d}u=\tfrac14-\tfrac13+\tfrac18=\tfrac1{24}∫01​(1−u2)2u3du=41​−31​+81​=241​ again. In (b), differentiate: tan⁡3xsec⁡2x+tan⁡5xsec⁡2x=tan⁡3xsec⁡2x (1+tan⁡2x)=tan⁡3xsec⁡4x\tan^3x\sec^2x+\tan^5x\sec^2x=\tan^3x\sec^2x\,(1+\tan^2x) =\tan^3x\sec^4xtan3xsec2x+tan5xsec2x=tan3xsec2x(1+tan2x)=tan3xsec4x.

Pitfalls

  • Using the half-angle identity on an odd power. It works, but slowly; split off one factor instead.

  • Losing the minus sign of  du=−sin⁡x  dx\,\mathrm{d}u=-\sin x\,\,\mathrm{d}xdu=−sinxdx. With u=cos⁡xu=\cos xu=cosx in (a) it gives −124-\tfrac1{24}−241​: a negative answer for an integrand that is positive on (0,π2)(0,\tfrac\pi2)(0,2π​).

  • Converting every power of sec⁡\secsec. In (b), sec⁡4x=(1+tan⁡2x)2\sec^4x=(1+\tan^2x)^2sec4x=(1+tan2x)2 leaves no sec⁡2x\sec^2xsec2x to make  du\,\mathrm{d}udu.

10.4 Trigonometric substitution

Problem. Integrate an expression containing a2−x2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}a2−x2​, a2+x2\sqrt{a^2+x^2}a2+x2​ or x2−a2\sqrt{x^2-a^2}x2−a2​ (or a power of a2+x2a^2+x^2a2+x2) that no plain substitution clears.

Method

  1. Read off the form and a>0a>0a>0, and substitute: a2−x2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}a2−x2​: x=asin⁡θx=a\sin\thetax=asinθ, θ∈[−π2,π2]\theta\in[-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2]θ∈[−2π​,2π​]; a2+x2\sqrt{a^2+x^2}a2+x2​: x=atan⁡θx=a\tan\thetax=atanθ, θ∈(−π2,π2)\theta\in(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)θ∈(−2π​,2π​); x2−a2\sqrt{x^2-a^2}x2−a2​ with x≥ax\ge ax≥a: x=asec⁡θx=a\sec\thetax=asecθ, θ∈[0,π2)\theta\in[0,\tfrac\pi2)θ∈[0,2π​).

  2. Write  dx\,\mathrm{d}xdx, and simplify the root by a Pythagorean identity. Use the range of θ\thetaθ to drop the modulus: a2−a2sin⁡2θ=a∣cos⁡θ∣=acos⁡θ\sqrt{a^2-a^2\sin^2\theta} =a\left|\cos\theta\right|=a\cos\thetaa2−a2sin2θ​=a∣cosθ∣=acosθ.

  3. Integrate in θ\thetaθ, often a trigonometric integral (Method 10.3). For a definite integral, change the limits to θ\thetaθ and finish there.

  4. For an indefinite integral, convert back to xxx: through the substitution and a right triangle, or algebraically (for instance cos⁡θ=1−sin⁡2θ\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}cosθ=1−sin2θ​ on the range).

  5. Add +C+C+C to an indefinite result.

Example Evaluate (a) ∫ dx(x2+1)2\displaystyle\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{(x^2+1)^2}∫(x2+1)2dx​ and (b) ∫01x24−x2  dx\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫01​4−x2​x2​dx.

(a) A power of a2+x2a^2+x^2a2+x2 with a=1a=1a=1: put x=tan⁡θx=\tan\thetax=tanθ, θ∈(−π2,π2)\theta\in(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)θ∈(−2π​,2π​), so  dx=sec⁡2θ  dθ\,\mathrm{d}x=\sec^2\theta\,\,\mathrm{d}\thetadx=sec2θdθ and (x2+1)2=sec⁡4θ(x^2+1)^2=\sec^4\theta(x2+1)2=sec4θ. Then, by the half-angle identity, ∫sec⁡2θsec⁡4θ  dθ=∫cos⁡2θ  dθ=12θ+14sin⁡2θ+C.\int\frac{\sec^2\theta}{\sec^4\theta}\,\,\mathrm{d}\theta=\int\cos^2\theta\,\,\mathrm{d}\theta =\tfrac12\theta+\tfrac14\sin2\theta+C .∫sec4θsec2θ​dθ=∫cos2θdθ=21​θ+41​sin2θ+C. Convert back: θ=arctan⁡x\theta=\arctan xθ=arctanx, and sin⁡2θ=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ=2tan⁡θsec⁡2θ=2x1+x2\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{\sec^2\theta}=\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}sin2θ=2sinθcosθ=sec2θ2tanθ​=1+x22x​. So the integral is 12arctan⁡x+x2(1+x2)+C\boxed{\tfrac12\arctan x+\frac{x}{2(1+x^2)}+C}21​arctanx+2(1+x2)x​+C​

(b) The form a2−x2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}a2−x2​ with a=2a=2a=2: put x=2sin⁡θx=2\sin\thetax=2sinθ, θ∈[−π2,π2]\theta\in[-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2]θ∈[−2π​,2π​], so  dx=2cos⁡θ  dθ\,\mathrm{d}x=2\cos\theta\,\,\mathrm{d}\thetadx=2cosθdθ and 4−x2=2cos⁡θ\sqrt{4-x^2}=2\cos\theta4−x2​=2cosθ. The limits: x=0↦θ=0x=0\mapsto\theta=0x=0↦θ=0, and x=1↦sin⁡θ=12x=1\mapsto \sin\theta=\tfrac12x=1↦sinθ=21​, so θ=π6\theta=\tfrac\pi6θ=6π​. Then ∫01x2  dx4−x2=∫0π/64sin⁡2θ⋅2cos⁡θ2cos⁡θ  dθ=∫0π/64sin⁡2θ  dθ=∫0π/62(1−cos⁡2θ)  dθ=[2θ−sin⁡2θ]0π/6,\begin{align*} \int_0^1\frac{x^2\,\,\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}} &=\int_0^{\pi/6}\frac{4\sin^2\theta\cdot2\cos\theta}{2\cos\theta}\,\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\ &=\int_0^{\pi/6}4\sin^2\theta\,\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\ &=\int_0^{\pi/6}2(1-\cos2\theta)\,\,\mathrm{d}\theta\\ &=\bigl[2\theta-\sin2\theta\bigr]_0^{\pi/6}, \end{align*}∫01​4−x2​x2dx​​=∫0π/6​2cosθ4sin2θ⋅2cosθ​dθ=∫0π/6​4sin2θdθ=∫0π/6​2(1−cos2θ)dθ=[2θ−sin2θ]0π/6​,​ which is π3−32≈0.181\boxed{\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2}\approx0.1813π​−23​​​≈0.181.

Check. In (a), differentiate, using the quotient rule on the second term: 12(1+x2)+1−x22(1+x2)2=1(1+x2)2.\frac{1}{2(1+x^2)}+\frac{1-x^2}{2(1+x^2)^2}=\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^2} .2(1+x2)1​+2(1+x2)21−x2​=(1+x2)21​. In (b), the integrand increases from 000 to 13≈0.577\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\approx0.5773​1​≈0.577 on [0,1][0,1][0,1], so the value must lie between 000 and 0.5770.5770.577; it does.

Pitfalls

  • Choosing by habit: 4−x2\sqrt{4-x^2}4−x2​ takes sin⁡\sinsin, x2−4\sqrt{x^2-4}x2−4​ takes sec⁡\secsec. With the wrong one no identity clears the root: x=2sin⁡θx=2\sin\thetax=2sinθ makes x2−4=−4cos⁡2θx^2-4=-4\cos^2\thetax2−4=−4cos2θ, which is negative.

  • Forgetting to change the limits in (b), or changing them and then converting back to xxx as well.

  • Using a trigonometric substitution where a plain one works: ∫x4−x2  dx\int x\sqrt{4-x^2}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫x4−x2​dx needs only u=4−x2u=4-x^2u=4−x2.

10.5 Improper integrals

Problem. Evaluate an integral over an unbounded interval, or of a function that is unbounded on a finite interval, or show that it diverges.

Method

  1. Replace ∞\infty∞ by ttt (and −∞-\infty−∞ by sss). Split a doubly infinite integral at any convenient point ccc into two pieces.

  2. Integrate on the finite interval, [a,t][a,t][a,t], as an ordinary definite integral.

  3. Take the limit t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞. Justify each term: a term such as t e−tt\,\mathrm{e}^{-t}te−t tends to 000 by l’Hôpital’s rule (Unit 8).

  4. State the verdict: the integral converges to the limit, or it diverges. A split integral converges only if each piece does.

Example Evaluate, or show divergent: (a) ∫−∞∞ dxx2−6x+13\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x^2-6x+13}∫−∞∞​x2−6x+13dx​ and (b) ∫2∞xx2+1  dx\displaystyle\int_2^{\infty}\frac{x}{x^2+1}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫2∞​x2+1x​dx.

(a) Complete the square: x2−6x+13=(x−3)2+4x^2-6x+13=(x-3)^2+4x2−6x+13=(x−3)2+4, so an antiderivative is 12arctan⁡x−32\tfrac12\arctan\tfrac{x-3}{2}21​arctan2x−3​. Split at c=3c=3c=3: ∫3t dxx2−6x+13=12arctan⁡t−32→π4,∫s3 dxx2−6x+13=−12arctan⁡s−32→π4,\begin{align*} \int_3^t\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x^2-6x+13}&=\tfrac12\arctan\tfrac{t-3}{2} \to\tfrac\pi4,\\ \int_s^3\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x^2-6x+13}&=-\tfrac12\arctan\tfrac{s-3}{2} \to\tfrac\pi4, \end{align*}∫3t​x2−6x+13dx​∫s3​x2−6x+13dx​​=21​arctan2t−3​→4π​,=−21​arctan2s−3​→4π​,​ as t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞ and s→−∞s\to-\inftys→−∞. Both pieces converge, so the integral converges to π4+π4=π2\tfrac\pi4+\tfrac\pi4=\boxed{\tfrac\pi2}4π​+4π​=2π​​.

(b) The numerator is half the derivative of the denominator: ∫2txx2+1  dx=[12ln⁡(x2+1)]2t=12ln⁡(t2+1)−12ln⁡5.\begin{align*} \int_2^t\frac{x}{x^2+1}\,\,\mathrm{d}x&=\Bigl[\tfrac12\ln(x^2+1)\Bigr]_2^t\\ &=\tfrac12\ln(t^2+1)-\tfrac12\ln5 . \end{align*}∫2t​x2+1x​dx​=[21​ln(x2+1)]2t​=21​ln(t2+1)−21​ln5.​ This grows without bound as t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞, so the integral diverges\boxed{\text{diverges}}diverges​.

Variants. An integrand that is unbounded at a point of a finite interval makes the integral improper too. At an endpoint aaa, integrate from sss and let s→a+s\to a^{+}s→a+; at an interior point ccc, split at ccc and require both halves to converge, since FTC 2 applied straight across the blow-up can return a finite but wrong answer. For instance, ∫−18 dxx23=lim⁡t→0−[3x3]−1t+lim⁡s→0+[3x3]s8=3+6=9.\begin{align*} \int_{-1}^{8}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt[3]{x^2}} &=\lim_{t\to0^-}\bigl[3\sqrt[3]{x}\bigr]_{-1}^{t}\\ &\quad+\lim_{s\to0^+}\bigl[3\sqrt[3]{x}\bigr]_{s}^{8}\\ &=3+6=9 . \end{align*}∫−18​3x2​dx​​=t→0−lim​[33x​]−1t​+s→0+lim​[33x​]s8​=3+6=9.​

Check. In (a), differentiate the antiderivative: the chain rule gives 12⋅12⋅1/(1+14(x−3)2)=1/((x−3)2+4)\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12\cdot1/\bigl(1+\tfrac14(x-3)^2\bigr)=1/\bigl((x-3)^2+4\bigr)21​⋅21​⋅1/(1+41​(x−3)2)=1/((x−3)2+4), the integrand; a missing 12\tfrac1221​ would double it. In (b), xx2+1≥12x\frac{x}{x^2+1}\ge\frac{1}{2x}x2+1x​≥2x1​ for x≥1x\ge1x≥1 (it rearranges to x2≥1x^2\ge1x2≥1), and the tail of 1x\frac1xx1​ has infinite area, so divergence is no surprise.

Pitfalls

  • Putting ∞\infty∞ into the formula as if it were a number. [⋅]2∞\bigl[\cdot\bigr]_2^\infty[⋅]2∞​ is only shorthand for the limit as t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞, taken after the integral is evaluated, and it has to be justified.

  • Deciding from the integrand alone. The integrand of (b) tends to 000, yet the integral diverges.

  • Evaluating a doubly infinite integral as one symmetric limit, lim⁡t→∞∫−tt\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_{-t}^{t}limt→∞​∫−tt​. That can be finite when the two halves diverge; take the pieces separately.

10.6 Setting up an integral by slice and sum

Problem. Turn a description into an integral: the area between two curves, the volume of a solid of revolution or of known cross-section, the work done lifting something, or the mass of a rod.

Method

  1. Say what xxx measures, from where, and the range it covers. For an area, find where the curves meet; sketch if asked.

  2. Write the contribution of one slice of width  dx\,\mathrm{d}xdx as (something)× dx(\text{something})\times\,\mathrm{d}x(something)×dx. A strip of height (top −-− bottom), with the top curve checked by a test point. A disc of area πf(x)2\pi f(x)^2πf(x)2. A slab of area A(x)A(x)A(x), by similar triangles if need be.   3. Integrate over the range. For an area, split at every crossing, so that each piece has the right curve on top.

10.7 Probability density: normalise, probability, expectation

Problem. A random quantity XXX has a density fff, perhaps with an unknown constant. Fix the constant, then find a probability and the expectation.

Method

  1. Check that fff is a density: f(x)≥0f(x)\ge0f(x)≥0, and ∫f=1\int f=1∫f=1 over its range. If fff contains an unknown constant kkk, impose ∫f=1\int f=1∫f=1 to find it.

  2. A probability is an area: P(a≤X≤b)=∫abf(x)  dxP(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^bf(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}xP(a≤X≤b)=∫ab​f(x)dx. Over an infinite range the integral is improper (Method 10.5).

  3. The expectation is E[X]=∫x f(x)  dx\mathbb{E}[X]=\int x\,f(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}xE[X]=∫xf(x)dx over the whole range. Over an infinite range it is improper too, and it must converge.

  4. Check: the probabilities of an event and of its complement add to 111, and E[X]\mathbb{E}[X]E[X] lies between the smallest and largest values XXX can take.

Example XXX has density f(x)=k(1+x)3f(x)=\dfrac{k}{(1+x)^3}f(x)=(1+x)3k​ on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞), and 000 elsewhere. Find kkk, P(X>1)P(X>1)P(X>1) and E[X]\mathbb{E}[X]E[X].

Normalise. An antiderivative of (1+x)−3(1+x)^{-3}(1+x)−3 is −12(1+x)−2-\tfrac12(1+x)^{-2}−21​(1+x)−2, so ∫0tk  dx(1+x)3=k2(1−1(1+t)2),\int_0^t\frac{k\,\,\mathrm{d}x}{(1+x)^3}=\frac k2\Bigl(1-\frac1{(1+t)^2}\Bigr),∫0t​(1+x)3kdx​=2k​(1−(1+t)21​), which tends to k2\tfrac k22k​ as t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞. Setting k2=1\tfrac k2=12k​=1 gives k=2\boxed{k=2}k=2​, and then f≥0f\ge0f≥0.

The probability is an improper integral: P(X>1)=lim⁡t→∞[−1(1+x)2]1t=0+14=14.P(X>1)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\Bigl[-\frac{1}{(1+x)^2}\Bigr]_1^t =0+\frac14=\boxed{\tfrac14} .P(X>1)=t→∞lim​[−(1+x)21​]1t​=0+41​=41​​.

For the mean, write x=(1+x)−1x=(1+x)-1x=(1+x)−1 in the numerator: 2x(1+x)3=2(1+x)2−2(1+x)3.\frac{2x}{(1+x)^3}=\frac{2}{(1+x)^2}-\frac{2}{(1+x)^3} .(1+x)32x​=(1+x)22​−(1+x)32​. Then ∫0t2x  dx(1+x)3=[−21+x+1(1+x)2]0t=−21+t+1(1+t)2+1,\begin{align*} \int_0^t\frac{2x\,\,\mathrm{d}x}{(1+x)^3} &=\Bigl[-\frac{2}{1+x}+\frac{1}{(1+x)^2}\Bigr]_0^t\\ &=-\frac{2}{1+t}+\frac{1}{(1+t)^2}+1 , \end{align*}∫0t​(1+x)32xdx​​=[−1+x2​+(1+x)21​]0t​=−1+t2​+(1+t)21​+1,​ which tends to 111 as t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞: E[X]=1\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X]=1}E[X]=1​.

Check. P(X≤1)=[−1(1+x)2]01=1−14=34P(X\le1)=\bigl[-\tfrac{1}{(1+x)^2}\bigr]_0^1=1-\tfrac14=\tfrac34P(X≤1)=[−(1+x)21​]01​=1−41​=43​, and 34+14=1\tfrac34+\tfrac14=143​+41​=1. For the mean, E[X]≥0\mathbb{E}[X]\ge0E[X]≥0 is a weak test, and 111 is also the value of ∫f\int f∫f, the first Pitfall’s wrong answer, so differentiate instead:  d dx(−21+x+1(1+x)2)=2(1+x)2−2(1+x)3\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\bigl(-\tfrac{2}{1+x}+\tfrac{1}{(1+x)^2}\bigr) =\tfrac{2}{(1+x)^2}-\tfrac{2}{(1+x)^3}dxd​(−1+x2​+(1+x)21​)=(1+x)22​−(1+x)32​, the split integrand.

Pitfalls

  • Finding E[X]\mathbb{E}[X]E[X] from ∫f\int f∫f instead of ∫xf\int x f∫xf. The first is 111 for every density.
